title: Two-Way Tables and Probability

explanation: A [[kw:two-way table]] (or contingency table) shows data that fits into two categories – one category forms the rows, the other the columns.
Each inside number is a [[kw:joint frequency]] – it counts how many individuals fall into both that row and column.
The totals along the bottom and right side are called [[kw:marginal frequencies]] – they sum up a whole row or column.
The grand total (bottom right corner) equals the total number of observations.
To complete a table, start by filling known joint frequencies, then subtract from marginal totals to find missing values.

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Joint frequency: count inside cells} $$ $$ \text{Marginal frequency: row or column sum} $$ $$ \text{Grand total: sum of all cells} $$
notes: All marginal totals must sum to the grand total.
formulaCard.title: Two-Way Table Terminology

discoveryHook.scenario: You survey your classmates: Do you play an instrument? Do you speak a foreign language? A two‑way table lets you organize the answers so you can see connections – like how many musicians are also bilingual – at a single glance!

steps: Grand total = 220.

The two column marginal relative frequencies (Attending + Not Attending) = 0.541 + 0.459 = 1.
0.541 is the proportion attending.

explanation: A [[kw:joint relative frequency]] is a joint frequency divided by the grand total – it tells what fraction of the whole group falls into that cell.
A [[kw:marginal relative frequency]] is a row or column total divided by the grand total – it gives the overall proportion for one category alone.
All joint relative frequencies sum to 1 (or 100%).
Relative frequencies can be written as fractions, decimals, or percents.

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Joint Relative Freq.} = \frac{\text{Joint Freq.}}{\text{Grand Total}} $$ $$ \text{Marginal Relative Freq.} = \frac{\text{Marginal Freq.}}{\text{Grand Total}} $$
notes: Each joint relative frequency is a probability estimate for that specific combination.
The grand total becomes 1 in the relative frequency table.

explanation: A [[kw:conditional relative frequency]] is the ratio of a joint relative frequency to the marginal relative frequency of the given condition (row or column).
It answers: 'Given that the individual is in this row/column, what is the chance they are in that column/row?'
Formula based on row totals: $$ \text{Cond. Rel. Freq.} = \frac{\text{Joint Relative Freq.}}{\text{Row Marginal Relative Freq.}} $$
You can also condition on columns.
These are essentially estimates of conditional probabilities.

formulaCard.title: Conditional Relative Frequency (Row-Based)
notes: The denominator is the 'given' group's relative size.
Row conditional frequencies sum to 1 across the row.
Similarly, for columns, divide by column marginal relative frequency.
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Cond. Rel. Freq.} = \frac{\text{Joint Relative Freq.}}{\text{Row Marginal Relative Freq.}} $$

confusionCorner.title: Which Total to Use?
confusionCorner.body: If the condition is a row (like 'given junior'), divide by the row total. If it's a column (like 'given attending'), divide by the column total. [[imp:Always match the denominator to the 'given' group.]]

confusionCorner.title: Don't Confuse Relative Frequency with Probability
confusionCorner.body: In a sample, relative frequencies estimate the true probabilities. When checking independence, use the relative frequencies from the sample and acknowledge they are estimates. [[imp:Small differences may not prove dependence; but large differences do.]]

questions.prompt: If P(A|B) = 0.3 and P(A) = 0.3, are A and B independent? Answer 'yes' or 'no'.
hints: Independence means the condition doesn't change the probability.
If P(A|B) equals P(A), events are independent.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: If P(A|B) = P(A), the events are independent, so yes.

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{If } P(B \mid A) \approx P(B) \text{, then A and B are independent.} $$
formulaCard.title: Independence Check from Table
notes: Use conditional probabilities based on row/column totals.
Alternatively, check if joint probability equals product of marginals.
In tables, these are the theoretical probabilities estimated by relative frequencies.

explanation: From a two-way table of relative frequencies, you can compute [[kw:conditional probabilities]] directly: $ P(B \mid A) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(A)} $.
To test independence of two events, check if $ P(B \mid A) = P(B) $, or equivalently, $ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) $.
When using a table, compare a conditional relative frequency to the corresponding marginal relative frequency; if they are equal (or very close), events are independent.
Real-world data often shows small differences due to sampling variability, but we look for approximate equality.

examples.prompt: Using the satellite TV table, determine if 'recommending' and 'living in Long Beach' are independent.
steps: P(Long Beach) = 0.36 (marginal).
P(Long Beach | yes) = P(yes & Long Beach)/P(yes) = 0.32 / 0.88 ≈ 0.3636.
Compare: 0.36 ≈ 0.3636, they are very close.
Because P(Long Beach) ≈ P(Long Beach | yes), the events are essentially independent.
examples.title: Example A – Testing Independence

examples.prompt: Check if recommending and living in Glendale are independent using the same table.
steps: P(Glendale) = 0.34.
P(Glendale | no) = P(no & Glendale)/P(no) = 0.05 / 0.12 ≈ 0.4167.
0.34 ≠ 0.4167, so there's a clear difference.
Thus, recommending and living in Glendale appear dependent (the no group has a higher Glendale proportion).
examples.title: Example B – Which City Shows Dependence?

steps: Total endangered = 70+80+318 = 468. Total species = sum all = 70+16+80+16+318+142 = 642.
0.729 ≠ 0.814, so they are not independent. Mammals have a higher rate of endangerment.

examples.prompt: In the music/language survey (80 students, 25 play instrument & speak language, 41 play instrument). Find P(speaks language | plays instrument).
steps: Understand: Given 'plays instrument', find probability of 'speaks language'.
Solve: P(speaks language | plays instrument) = (plays & speaks) / (total plays instrument) = 25/41.
Conclude: About 61% of instrumentalists also speak a foreign language.

steps: Understand: We need to see if P(speaks | plays) equals P(speaks).
Solve: P(speaks) = 34/80 = 0.425. P(speaks | plays) = 25/41 ≈ 0.61.
Since 0.425 ≠ 0.61, they are not independent.
Conclude: Instrumentalists are more likely to speak a language than the general student body.

explanation: 1. [[imp:Understand]]: Identify the two categories and the specific event. Is it a joint probability (and) or a conditional probability (given)?
2. [[imp:Solve]]: Locate the needed frequencies – joint, marginal, or conditional. Use the appropriate formula: P(A and B) = joint freq / grand total; P(B|A) = joint freq of A&B / marginal freq of A.
3. [[imp:Conclude]]: State the probability in context, and if asked, check for independence by comparing with the relevant marginal.
